thread.title: The 30+1 Portfolio: An Average Investor's Reasoning For Buying A Stock - My Investment And Other Vehicles To Ensure My Retirement And Legacy

author: Sleeps Well At Night
title: The 30+1 Portfolio: An Average Investor's Reasoning For Buying A Stock - My Investment And Other Vehicles To Ensure My Retirement And Legacy
text:
First, I would like to thank everyone for the thoughts, comments, and support relating to my very first article published on Seeking Alpha.
With that, they always say the sequel is never as good as the original.
Source
However, I'm ready to tackle my second attempt to keep the Seeking Alpha community, and just as importantly, the people who have chosen to follow me, informed and hopefully entertained.
Targets One of the threads that occurred in the comments section in my last article centered around goals and targets. In the thread, a reader asked me about any specific goals I had as I talked about investing but did not mention or list any. He used the term "aimless investing". My first thought was of course I have goals. What kind of question is that? However, the one thing I have learned is to take a deep breath and invoke the twenty four hour rule if something initially rubs you the wrong way. As I thought about it more, the reader brought up good points. In my mind I had a set of targets. However, I have never written down my targets, on my own or in the article. To some if not most people, reading my initial article about investing without understanding my targets might look like this
Great, you have targets. Get to the point. What are they? Having liquid savings for unseen events by having an emergency fund.
Source
The one thing I've learned after reading books on investing and personal finance is have an emergency fund. Earlier in my career, I had to dip into my 401( K ) and credit cards multiple times for things these days I wouldn't even think twice about paying cash for or leveraging my credit card and paying off the balance the following month. What's my target with the emergency fund? To never, ever, tap into tax deferred accounts or credit cards again to cover short or medium term FUBAR events. As of today, I have four months of expenses with 59% in a liquid bank account and 41% in a taxable brokerage account. I know this will generate some discussion as 100% should be in a liquid bank account. It should be not about return, but safety and liquidity. Fortunately or unfortunately, my personality type and thought processes don't currently grant me the discipline to sit on this amount of cash and not try to "juice the return". I am auto contributing to the cash portion of the emergency fund every month which will lower the brokerage account percentage moving forward. The 41% in my brokerage account is spread out evenly among NFLX, MO, V, and MSFT. I know this one account is pretty concentrated in terms of number of stocks owned, but overall, my portfolio of assets is diverse in terms of number of stocks, index funds, and liquid assets.
Having more financial flexibility by having no long term credit card debt
I use one credit card for daily expenses and an Amazon Credit Card for the 5% back if I buy something on Amazon. I pay the balances off every month on these two cards. More disposable income means more financial flexibility. No credit card debt is by and far the most powerful target I hit and continue to hit that allows me to sleep well at night.
Funding future healthcare costs by having a Healthcare Spending Account ( HSA )
My company just instituted a HSA plan in 2018. What's a HSA?
A type of savings account that lets you set aside money on a pre-tax basis to pay for qualified medical expenses. By using untaxed dollars in a Health Savings Account (NYSE: HSA ) to pay for deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, and some other expenses, you can lower your overall health care costs.
An HSA can be used only if you have a High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) — generally any health plan (including a Marketplace plan) with a deductible of at least $1,350 for an individual or $2,700 for a family. When you view plans in the Marketplace, you can see if they’re "HSA-eligible."
For 2018, you can contribute up to $3,450 for self-only HDHP coverage and up to $6,900 for family HDHP coverage. HSA funds roll over year to year if you don't spend them.
An HSA may earn interest, which is not taxable. Some health insurance companies offer HSAs for their high deductible plans. Check with your company. You can also open an HSA through some banks and other financial institutions.
Source
I am having a set dollar amount sent to my HSA every pay period. How does this help me achieve my target of funding my healthcare costs once I retire?
All non employer contributed dollars are deductible up to the $6900.00 per year for a family. Any interest, capital gains, and / or dividends are not taxable. Any withdrawals used for qualified healthcare expenses are not taxed My HSA allows me to takes the monies and invest in mutual funds or target funds. There are no forced withdrawals upon retirement or by a certain age. My strategy is to pay for all out of pocket expenses now and not use the funds until retirement. If I save all the receipts that I incur from now until retirement, I can start withdrawing funds and pay myself back. However, since I have already paid the out of pocket, I can pretty much use any funds I withdraw upon retirement for anything as long as they match my saved medical receipts.
My takeaway is if you are in a HDHP and have access to a HSA, seriously consider if this type of plan will fit your current situation.
Helping fund Junior's college fund utilizing a 529 plan with a UTMA thrown in for beer money Source
The plan is for Junior to go to college. Since he is only ten years old, who knows what he's going to decide down the road. Given that, it's better to assume he's going to pursue higher education versus going down a different path and not planning for it. If he does go down a different path, I'll support those decisions as long as he's happy and does no harm to himself or others socially or economically.
If you can't help yourself, how can you help others?
Will I be able fund his whole college education? Maybe. The one thing I do know is that he will probably be able to get loans and /or scholarships for any gaps that can't be filled. I on the other hand am 100% certain that no reputable financial institution will lend me any money to retire.
Beer Money in the form of a UTMA
Source
He also has a UTMA set up for beer money. Hopefully he will choose to use it for something else. His UTMA consists of AAPL, MSFT, DNKN, PFE, T, and USB. However, this is a good example of understanding the product you're using and investing in. The goal was to use the UTMA for college not understanding that it is an irrevocable gift and Junior can use it anyway he wants to when he turns eighteen. That's why I call it his beer money.
If life deals you melons - you probably have dyslexia
The one good thing concerning this mistake is that I have started teaching the little guy about stocks and dividends. He picked DNKN because he likes Baskin Robbins ice cream and APPL because he's always on his damn iPad. His picks are up 21% and 66% respectively. I picked MSFT, PFE, USB, and Grandpa picked T.
Funding my retirement and future legacy utilizing my company 401( K ) and rollover IRA While my first and future articles will focus on management of my rollover IRA, my largest retirement tool is my current company 401( K ) which has a larger balance than the rollover and is a beast that is constantly being fed every pay period.
The company matches the first 4% of my contributions at 100% I am currently contributing 15% of my salary including the company match The split is 12% tax deferred including company match / 3% taxable I have auto increase at 1% a year on the Roth 401 up to 9% which would equal the max I can contribute of 17% which with 4% company match equals 21% I have a choice of index funds and / or target date funds The current allocation is 25% International Stock Index Fund, 25% S & P 500 Fund, 25% Bond Index Fund, and 25% Russell 2000 Fund I look forward to comments and suggestions concerning allocation and whether to start being more heavily weighted in the Roth 401( K ) vs the Traditional 401( K ) if anyone is still reading
Last but not least Ensuring my legacy lives on with a well executed estate plan Source
Everyone dies, for now at least. I kept putting this part off because who wants to plan for their own death? However, the older I get and the older Junior gets, the more I started thinking about ensuring he is taken care of and the assets I worked so hard for are distributed as efficiently and advantageously as possible. Personally, I don't want the government and the court systems determining the future of the family tree.
At this point, if you don't have an estate plan, you should at least start thinking about it and whether it fits your particular situation.
The Big Finale Here it is, article #2 or maybe it's article #1 (2 of 2). Hopefully you have found this article interesting as a wraparound to my first article.
While not as heavy on any particular investment thesis or company, the reader's comments and thoughts from the first article necessitated I write a follow up so that people who decide to follow me and /or read and comment on possible future articles have a deeper understanding of my thought process being an average investor.
Thanks for reading and I look forward to comments and insights on the above.
